findings.reason: client-go already returns secret.Data decoded. isBase64 accepts any string whose length is a multiple of 4 and that uses only [A-Za-z0-9+/=]. The operator generates 16-character passwords from letters, digits and !@#$%^&* (utils/kubernetes.py:1428-1429), so the all-alphanumeric ones decode cleanly into 12 garbage bytes and authentication fails.
findings.claim: decodeSecretKey base64-decodes a second time any secret value that looks like base64, which corrupts many real passwords.
findings.evidence: client-go already returns `secret.Data` decoded. `if isBase64(decoded) { if b, err := base64.StdEncoding.DecodeString(decoded); err == nil { return string(b), nil } }` then decodes again any value whose length is a multiple of 4 and which contains only [A-Za-z0-9+/=]. The operator generates passwords as 16 characters from `ascii_letters + digits + "!@#$%^&*"` (src/keycloak_operator/utils/kubernetes.py:1428-1429). About (62/70)^16 ≈ 14% of those are pure alphanumeric, and every such value is valid unpadded base64, so the password becomes 12 garbage bytes. A username like `root` or an existingSecret password like `Passw0rdPassw0rd` is mangled the same way. The "double-encoding" case it claims to guard against cannot work anyway: the operator decodes existingSecret values once and passes them to Keycloak unchanged (keycloak_reconciler.py:1315-1320).

members.claim: decodeSecretKey base64-decodes a second time any secret value that happens to look like base64. Many real admin passwords and usernames get turned into random bytes, so authentication fails with 401 in cluster mode.
